papers.title: Primary stability of short implants compared with standard implants placed with a simulated closed sinus floor elevation technique: an in vitro study
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Primary implant stability is a key determinant of successful osseointegration, particularly in the posterior maxilla, where bone quality is often compromised. Short implants have been proposed as an alternative to sinus floor elevation; however, data comparing their primary stability with that of standard implants placed using closed sinus floor elevation remain limited. This in vitro study aimed to compare the primary stability of short and standard implants. Materials and methods An in vitro experimental model was used to assess primary implant stability. Short implants and standard implants placed following simulated closed sinus floor elevation were evaluated using resonance frequency analysis and Periotest measurements ( n = 40). Implant stability values were obtained from frontal and lateral directions, with five readings averaged in each direction for every implant. Descriptive statistics were calculated, and group comparisons were performed. Pearson correlation analysis was used to evaluate relationships between measurement directions within each implant group and between assessment methods. Results No statistically significant differences in primary stability were observed between short implants and standard implants based on either resonance frequency analysis or Periotest measurements ( p > 0.05). Conclusions Within the limitations of this in vitro model, no statistically significant difference in primary stability was detected between short and standard implants under similar crestal bone engagement. As healing, secondary stability, and loading were not assessed, clinical studies are required to confirm these findings. Trial registration Not applicable.

papers.title: Experiment-compatible measurement-feedback quantum state preparation with reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Ground-state preparation is a critical task in quantum simulation and quantum computing, as it enables the study of correlated phases and the generation of entangled resource states. While measurement–feedback control has emerged as a promising route to state preparation, existing schemes either rely on handcrafted, task-specific policies or are designed using full quantum-state information that is unavailable in real experiments and becomes impractical for large many-body systems. Here we develop an adaptive measurement–feedback protocol based on reinforcement learning under partial observability. The controller uses only the history of experimentally accessible measurement outcomes to choose both the measurement operator and the feedback action in real time. To make training compatible with experiments, we introduce a stochastic terminal reward built from one-shot measurements of randomly sampled Hamiltonian components, avoiding unphysical full-state reconstruction while remaining an unbiased estimator of the target energy. We demonstrate the method by preparing ground states of the Bose–Hubbard model and by generating GHZ states, establishing a scalable and hardware-compatible route to quantum state preparation.

papers.title: A novel strategy for reconstruction of AORI type III proximal tibial defects
papers.abstract: Aims For cases of Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute (AORI) type III proximal tibial defects with intact medial collateral ligaments (MCLs), knee reconstruction is conventionally performed using semi-constrained prostheses with stemmed tibial components in conjunction with cones or sleeves. This study aimed to reconstruct AORI type III tibial defects using a 3D-printed extension-stem augment, followed by surface-type knee reconstruction to achieve long-term stability and promising clinical outcomes. Methods A patient-specific porous extension-stem augment was designed based on the defect morphology. The microporous structure allowed direct contact for osseointegration, the proximal portion supported tibial baseplate, while the distal stem achieved intramedullary fixation. Finite element analysis (FEA) assessed the biomechanical stability of the augment. A retrospective analysis was conducted between July 2021 and September 2023 on patients who underwent reconstruction of AORI type III proximal tibial defects with extension-stem augment and surface-type total knee prosthesis. Results FEA demonstrated favourable stress and strain distribution and micromotion at the prosthesis-bone interface, although localized high-strain regions were observed under higher-demand loading conditions. Four patients (0 male, 4 female) were included, with a minimum follow-up of 20.7 months (20.7 to 30) and a median age at surgery of 63.0 years (IQR 60.3 to 66.3). The mean Knee Society Score (KSS) improved significantly to 85 (82 to 87), and the mean Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score decreased by 18 (16 to 20). One patient developed periprosthetic joint infection on the femoral side at 20.7 months postoperatively and underwent revision surgery. Intraoperatively, the augment was securely integrated and could not be extracted. Radiological evaluation demonstrated satisfactory alignment and joint stability, with no evidence of prosthesis loosening or migration at the latest follow-up. Conclusion The extension-stem augment achieved anatomical reconstruction of AORI type III proximal tibial defects and provided stable support for the surface-type prosthesis, ensuring reliable knee stability after reconstruction. This represents a feasible option for revision of AORI type III tibial defects. Cite this article: Bone Joint Res 2026;15(10):1263–1273.

papers.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

papers.title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
papers.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $π_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/.

papers.title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting
papers.abstract: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.

papers.title: Continuous-Time Policy Gradient from Discrete Data: Convergence Analysis and Model-Free Algorithms
papers.abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning seeks an optimal policy under unknown dynamics driven by stochastic differential equations using observations collected at discrete times. We develop a policy gradient framework that combines rigorous convergence analysis with learning from discrete data. We first establish a performance difference lemma and derive policy gradient formulas for randomized and parametrized policies. We then prove exponential convergence of an entropy-regularized policy flow to the regularized optimum. For discrete parametrized updates, we derive a convergence bound that explicitly separates the contributions of critic error, policy-regression error, and the learning step size. To enable learning under unknown dynamics, we integrate this framework with PhiBE, which constructs a continuous-time surrogate generator from discrete transition data. The resulting on-policy and off-policy model-free actor-critic algorithms preserve the continuous-time structure of the control problem. Numerical experiments on an entropy-regularized linear-quadratic regulator and a nonlinear wheeled robot demonstrate the performance and stability of the proposed methods with both known and data-driven dynamics.

papers.title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See
papers.abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.

papers.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

papers.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
papers.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.

papers.title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning
papers.abstract: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.

papers.title: Physical AI for Intralogistics: Benchmarking the NVIDIA Sim-to-Real Ecosystem for Cosmos-Enhanced COMPASS Navigation on Industrial Mobile Robots
papers.abstract: Classical robot navigation stacks are reliable but often require re-engineering for each new robot type and site. Learning-based navigation shifts this effort from hand-tuned parameters to data generation and training, where a policy adapts to each new embodiment or facility by fine-tuning in simulation. Whether policies adapted this way stay reliable on real industrial robots has seen little systematic testing. We study this for NVIDIA's X-Mobility and COMPASS workflow for training learned navigation policies on Idealworks robots. In simulation, we extend the COMPASS benchmark with two embodiments, the differential-drive iw.hub and an omnidirectional Humanoid Mobile Platform (HMP), and with a digital twin of the Idealworks R&D center. For the real world, we fine-tune X-Mobility on data from this digital twin, with and without sim-to-real variants generated by NVIDIA Cosmos, train COMPASS on top of it from scratch in the digital twin, deploy the resulting policies on the iw.hub's onboard Jetson AGX Xavier, and benchmark them in the Idealworks R&D center against COMPASS trained only on NVIDIA's environments and the existing Idealworks navigation stack on task success, efficiency, safety, smoothness and onboard compute. Running every static scenario both in a digital-twin replica and in the real facility measures the sim-to-real gap and how far Cosmos-augmented data closes it. Training in the digital twin with Cosmos sim-to-real augmentation raises the real-world success rate of learned navigation from 65.3% to 91.7% across four scenarios and nearly halves its weighted travel time compared with simulation-only training, bringing it within 8.3 points of the production navigation stack, fully onboard; with an integrated global planner, it also reaches far, occluded goals in every trial.

papers.title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

papers.title: SPAR: Search-trained Push Action Ranker for Efficient Navigation Among Movable Obstacles
papers.abstract: Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) requires a robot to rearrange objects that block access to its goal. For a pushing robot, progress may depend on a setup push that enables a later opening without itself clearing a passage. The number of candidate sequences can grow exponentially with sequence length, making physics-based search costly. We introduce the Search-trained Push Action Ranker (SPAR), which learns to prioritize push primitives from simulated search outcomes. Searches over sequences of up to two pushes per object provide supervision that distinguishes immediate openings from setup pushes. A transformer trained with regression and ranking losses scores primitives using contact tokens conditioned on scene geometry and reachability regions. The same model guides simulator evaluations in SPAR Search and selects actions for direct execution in SPAR Policy. Both modes solve successive keyhole problems that open access to neighboring free-space regions within a NAMO planner. Across successful runs on $300$ simulated two-push keyhole problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls by $7.0\times$, leading to a $3.8\times$ reduction in planning time relative to Random Search. Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on $600$ keyhole problems which have no solution within two pushes. At a depth limit of five pushes, SPAR Search achieves $50.7\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $20.2\%$ for Random Search. These gains carry over to NAMO planning: on hard simulated scenes, SPAR Search achieves $47\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $21\%$ for Random Search. In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy succeeds in $37/40$ trials without a physics-based digital twin, compared with $33/40$ for SPAR Search and $27/40$ for Random Search.

papers.title: Reinforced Iterative Learning Control for elastic joint arms: Guaranteed cross-trajectory generalization under model uncertainties
papers.abstract: Trajectory tracking for compliant robots is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and modeling uncertainties, often requiring learning-based methods to avoid explicit parameter identification. Iterative Learning Control (ILC) ensures theoretically high precision and preserves the passive compliance of the robot. However, traditional ILC requires a separate learning phase for each new trajectory. Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) generalizes to new trajectories, but practically suffers from high sample complexity and limited tracking precision. This work proposes Reinforced Iterative Learning Control (RILC) that combines the strengths of both approaches to achieve fast adaptation and guaranteed tracking convergence across diverse trajectories. By establishing a concurrent coupling between the two controllers, RILC overcomes the high initial errors and slow adaptation of traditional ILC, enabling high-performance tracking from the very first trials. In this architecture, ILC provides high-quality samples, while RL contributes as a generalizing best-effort policy across iterations. Additionally, a theoretical proof is presented to show that the RL component preserves ILC stability and, under specific conditions, can also reduce the error bound asymptotically. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-degree-of-freedom serial elastic robot using different trajectories and modeling mismatches.

papers.title: Manifold-Informed Neural Networks for Low-Label ECG Electrolyte Inference
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_φ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_φ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Block Selection for Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGPs) are a widely used, principled approach to scalable Gaussian process modelling. Their success stems from their theoretically interpretable structure: they provide a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the full GP while allowing scal- able stochastic optimization. Recent work has explored modifications of the posterior conditional distribution and has shown that such extensions can improve upon this well-established framework. In particular, introducing a block-diagonal structured scal- ing matrix leads to a tighter lower bound on the GP marginal likelihood. We investigate whether selecting blocks that tighten the variational objective improves test RMSE and NLL at a fixed inducing-point budget. Since the scaling matrix contributes to the variational lower bound through an upper bound on the log-determinant of the full residual covariance matrix, our work makes the following contributions. First, we introduce a simple, scalable, geometry-aware algorithm, with explicit computational complexity and low computational overhead, that recovers a large fraction of this log- determinant contribution by selecting an appropriate partition of the data. Second, we show how to train these models using a doubly stochastic optimization framework. Finally, we investigate how sparse GP methods based on alternative conditional posterior structures can be used to learn better hyperparameters and inducing points for SVGP.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Regret Bounds for UCB-Style Gaussian Process Bandits via Data Thinning
papers.abstract: Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) has been widely studied, though its known regret upper bound is suboptimal. To obtain near-optimal regret upper bounds, existing studies mainly focus on non-adaptive methods, such as uncertainty sampling, whose practical effectiveness is often limited. This paper shows that, under a Gaussian noise assumption, UCB-style algorithms can achieve near-optimal regret upper bounds via data thinning, a statistical technique for creating independent datasets from a single dataset. First, we show that data thinning can yield tighter confidence intervals in the bandit setting, and that a direct extension of GP-UCB achieves a near-optimal simple regret upper bound. Furthermore, by leveraging the tighter confidence intervals and combining GP-UCB with a phased elimination algorithm, we show a near-optimal cumulative regret upper bound. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of UCB-style algorithms incorporating data thinning via numerical experiments.

papers.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
papers.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

papers.title: A Process-Informed, Photorealistic Digital Twin for Vision-Based Inline Inspection of C-SMC Strip Deposition
papers.abstract: Inline quality assurance for Sheet Molding Compound (SMC) manufacturing is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately labeled image datasets for training machine-learning models. This work presents a process-informed, photorealistic digital twin for carbon-fiber SMC strip deposition. A rigid-body simulation reproduces the deposition kinematics (settling, friction, belt motion), while a physically grounded polarization-rendering model produces realistic appearance, so that every image carries exact, mutually consistent labels in synchronized formats: oriented bounding boxes, point annotations, density maps, and polarization renderings (Angle and Degree of Linear Polarization). Because the joint distribution of many overlapping strips cannot be specified analytically, simulation yields exact, scalable ground truth that manual annotation cannot provide. The twin produces over 16,000 images across 3,300 frames, and the synthetic data replicate near-isotropic fiber orientation (axial concentration r < 0.05) consistent with as-deposited commercial SMC. Trained purely on synthetic data, YOLOv11 and CSRNet reach detection mAP50 up to 0.91, with a dedicated oriented-bounding-box detector confirming the oriented labels are directly trainable (mAP50 = 0.83); on real manufacturing images, the synthetic-to-real difference in edge and texture structure (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.46, distribution overlap 0.56) is of the same magnitude as the difference between two real acquisition series of the same material (0.41, overlap 0.57). The approach substantially reduces the labeling burden for camera-based inline inspection of fiber orientation and volume content.

papers.title: Knowing When to Stop Thinking: A Dissection of Expected Free Energy as a Test-Time Compute Controller for Latent World-Model Planning
papers.abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.

papers.title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints
papers.abstract: We consider the following inverse domain uncertainty quantification problem: given a prescribed value or measurement of a hemodynamic biomarker, characterize the distribution of vascular geometries compatible with it. The problem is formulated as a Bayesian inverse problem in which a high-dimensional latent parameter encodes the cardiovascular shape and accounts for inter-patient variability. The parameter-to-observable map composes a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant generating the aortic surface with a high-performance numerical finite element solver for the unsteady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations, from which biomarkers of interest are evaluated. The map is nonlinear, high-dimensional and computationally expensive. To address the problem, we compare three ensemble strategies: ensemble adjusted Kalman inversion (EAKI), adaptive Bayesian updating with structural reliability (aBUS), and a Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The first two approaches are derivative-free. For the third method, we introduce a novel differentiable flow-matching surrogate that reduces the cost of a single forward map evaluation at the price of a distribution shift depending on the training distribution used for the surrogate. We apply the framework to the generation of virtual patient cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops along aortic geometries affected by coarctation, and we validate and compare the three methods on synthetic data.

papers.title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.

papers.title: Practical Advantages of Online Conformal Prediction for Data Streams
papers.abstract: Full conformal prediction offers finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but exact computation can be costly, while its classical guarantees do not directly extend to non-stationary data streams. We compare four sequential conformal regression procedures with a weighted full-conformal benchmark in terms of empirical coverage, prediction interval width, and computational cost. The procedures combine ordinary or forgetting-factor least squares with uniform or exponentially weighted empirical residual quantiles, or with online gradient-based quantile tracking. Experiments cover an independent and identically distributed control, two synthetic distribution-shift scenarios, and four real-world data streams. Adapting the regression model as well as the conformal threshold substantially improves the coverage--width tradeoff under drift. The quantile-tracking procedure requires $O(p^2)$ time and memory per observation, independently of stream length, although its coverage can deteriorate after abrupt changes. These results illustrate the practical tradeoffs between predictor adaptation, uncertainty quantification, and computational resources.

papers.title: Prescribed Performance Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Roundabout Navigation of Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC's trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25\% increase in average success rate and a 65.87\% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.

papers.title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., "find a bed") in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.

papers.title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
papers.abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

papers.title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.

papers.title: Divide-and-Conquer Neural Bayes Estimation for Spatial and Spatiotemporal Point Process Models
papers.abstract: Spatial and spatiotemporal point process models are widely used to analyze event data across many scientific disciplines, but likelihood-based Bayesian inference is often computationally prohibitive due to intractable likelihoods, high-dimensional latent structures, and dependence on event history. Existing approximate and likelihood-free methods mitigate some of these challenges, but often at the cost of reduced statistical efficiency, imperfect uncertainty quantification, or information loss from reliance on predefined summary statistics. A promising recent approach involves neural networks, but it has only been explored in purely spatial or temporal settings and requires a computationally expensive training stage for large domains or dense point patterns. Here, we propose a divide-and-conquer neural Bayes estimation framework for spatial and spatiotemporal point process models. Our method operates directly on raw point pattern realizations using transformer-based architectures on partitions of the spatiotemporal domain, together with an attention mechanism to optimally combine locally extracted summaries. Simulation studies demonstrate reliable inference with improved scalability relative to existing general-purpose neural inference approaches and classical likelihood-based methods. We further demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach through an analysis of whale call data in Cape Cod Bay, MA, where, once trained, the estimator yields parameter estimates and credible intervals at negligible computational cost.

papers.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $ε$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

papers.title: From POMDP Theory to Deep RL with Particle Filters
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning in partially observable environments requires inferring hidden states, learning latent dynamics, and planning under the resulting belief. Practical algorithms often solve one aspect of the above pipeline while relying on approximations for the others that are often poorly understood, while existing POMDP theory typically analyzes computationally inefficient theoretical algorithms far from modern deep RL practice. To fill this gap, we propose a practical end-to-end algorithm that approximately solves the hidden state filtering problem via sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), updates a latent dynamics model online, and performs approximate online planning for $d$ steps before bootstrapping leaves with a state-value critic (a QMDP approximation). We analyze each approximation and prove an end-to-end regret bound decomposing the error into model estimation error, particle filter error, Monte Carlo rollout error, and a structural bias term induced by the QMDP approximation controllable by the planning depth that we further analyze in various special cases. The resulting guarantee makes explicit how statistical sample size, particle budget, rollout budget, and planning depth affect performance. We instantiate our algorithm in an MPC-based deep RL framework, demonstrating its practicality on a variety of environments. On a POMDP that satisfies our assumptions, each term of the bound decays at its predicted rate. Our results provide a practical and theoretically grounded route for bridging theory and practice within online decision-making in POMDPs.

papers.title: Active Pilot Sampling for Multi-fidelity Estimation in Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: Stochastic optimization with high-fidelity nonlinear models is often computationally prohibitive because each objective evaluation requires sampling-based uncertainty quantification inside an outer optimization loop. Multi-fidelity estimators, such as approximate control variates (ACV), can reduce this cost by exploiting cheaper low-fidelity models, but they require model-output covariance information to determine control-variate weights and sample allocations. These covariances are generally unknown and must be estimated through pilot sampling. Existing pilot-sampling strategies primarily address one-off estimation and do not exploit the structure of iterative stochastic optimization, where covariance information may vary smoothly across the design domain and can be shared across optimization queries. We propose an active pilot-sampling framework that learns a probabilistic emulator of the model-output covariance matrix using a positive-definite parameterization based on matrix-logarithm-transformed correlations and log standard deviations. The emulator provides design-specific covariance estimates for constructing ACV estimators at new optimization queries, avoiding repeated independent covariance estimation at every design. Active-learning acquisition functions allocate pilot samples to designs where covariance information is most uncertain and most relevant to the outer optimization objective. We demonstrate the method on a four-branch benchmark and a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimal experimental design application for sensor placement and measurement-time selection in a convection-diffusion system. The results show improved optimization performance relative to single-fidelity Monte Carlo and simpler pilot-sampling strategies.

papers.title: HypoNet Nankai PS: rapid hypocenter determination for the Nankai Trough using physics-informed neural networks with three-dimensional P- and S-wave velocity models
papers.abstract: Rapid and accurate hypocenter determination based on three-dimensional (3D) seismic velocity models is essential for seismic monitoring in subduction zones, yet it remains computationally demanding. HypoNet Nankai, a hypocenter determination package that uses physics-informed neural network (PINN) travel-time inference for a realistic 3D P-wave velocity model of the Nankai Trough subduction zone, was designed to address this problem, but supported only P-wave arrival times. Here, we present HypoNet Nankai PS, which extends the framework to both P- and S-wave travel times. We first constructed an S-wave velocity model from the existing P-wave model using empirical conversion relations for marine sediments and the crust. Because the resulting S-wave velocity structure has lower velocities and therefore considerably steeper travel-time gradients, the original PINN training procedure designed for the P-wave velocity structure was insufficient. We therefore revised the training procedure by reconsidering the distribution of collocation points, the NN architecture, and the optimizer. Benchmark comparisons with the fast marching method showed that the revised approach substantially reduced the root-mean-square deviations for both P- and S-waves compared with the original algorithm. Recovery tests using synthetic earthquakes were also performed. When applied to 223 earthquakes recorded by DONET stations off the Kii Peninsula, the system yielded hypocenters generally consistent with the JMA catalog beneath the network, suggesting that the 3D velocity model captures travel-time variations accommodated by JMA's 1D model and station corrections. Farther seaward, the estimated hypocenters were substantially shallower than those in the JMA catalog and were located in the oceanic crust and uppermost mantle, consistent with previous relocations that used DONET data and 3D velocity models.

llm.relevance_to_user: 该文用PINN在三维速度模型中快速求解走时与震源，属于用神经网络替代昂贵正演/反演的代理建模思路，可迁移到FEA代理与生物力学参数反演，但应用领域为地震学。

papers.title: Soliton Profiles in 1D: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers and Constrained Deep Ritz Methods
papers.abstract: We develop and compare enhanced neural-network solvers for one-dimensional ground-state profiles, which are solutions of $$ Q^{\prime\prime}=bQ-γQ^{p},\quad Q>0,\quad p>1, \quad b, γ>0, $$ the stationary profile equation for the nonlinear Schrödinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations. Its explicit sech-type solutions serve as exact reference for error computation and benchmark hyperparameter selection. We improve on the standard Adam-trained physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline by introducing higher-order optimization via Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS refinements, as well as Fourier-feature PINNs, and constrained Deep Ritz (DR) formulations. In DR approaches we introduce two new neural-network formulations, which implement two classical variational characterizations: a Nehari-constrained Deep Ritz method, in which the height is learned by projecting onto the Nehari/Pokhozhaev manifold, and a Weinstein Deep Ritz method, in which a normalized profile minimizes the Weinstein quotient. The Deep Ritz formulations perform best overall, in particular, the Weinstein variant gives the best error-runtime balance. The neural-network based solvers remain less accurate and efficient than classical Petviashvili iteration in 1D, however, the current study provides a proof of concept: the mesh-free formulation, non-reliance on exact profiles or the related features make them promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.

papers.title: Using Set Learning to Improve Set-Valued Classifiers on Long-tailed Data
papers.abstract: Set-valued classification (SVC) offers a practical approach to communicating uncertainty while maintaining accuracy by predicting variable-sized sets per input rather than fixed-sized sets (e.g. top-1 or top-5). However, set-valued classifiers (SVCs) exhibit significantly degraded performance on long-tailed and imbalanced datasets, a setting for which they are ostensibly well-suited. This becomes apparent under macro-average evaluation, which weighs all classes equally. SVCs are typically formed during a post-hoc calibration stage, so little is known about how training dynamics affect their behaviour. In this work, we investigate how different neural network training strategies and loss functions impact downstream SVC performance on highly imbalanced data. In addition to methods such as label smoothing and class-balancing, we investigate whether loss functions that operate over sets of examples in a batch, rather than treating all examples as independent, lead to better downstream SVCs. We adapt the recently proposed odd-K-out (OKO) loss function, which learns from sets of training samples, improving its sample efficiency whilst introducing algorithmic modifications that reduce its computational overhead from 3.2x to just 1.36x that of standard cross-entropy training. Experiments on highly long-tailed datasets demonstrate our modified OKO approach significantly improves macro-accuracy across multiple SVC methods - including top-k, average-k, and conformal prediction - while maintaining competitive micro-accuracy. This improved performance on minority classes occurs without substantially increasing prediction set sizes, suggesting that carefully constructed set-based training can produce networks better suited to imbalanced data.

papers.title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
papers.abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.

papers.title: Extrusion-based additive manufacturing of zinc bone scaffolds based on triply periodic minimal surfaces
papers.abstract: Extrusion-based additive manufacturing is an emerging approach for fabricating architecturally complex biodegradable metallic bone implants, enabling zinc (Zn) to be processed into intricate scaffold architectures. Here, triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) Zn scaffolds with gyroid, diamond, and I-WP architectures were fabricated by extrusion-based additive manufacturing followed by debinding and sintering. Scaffolds with solid fractions of 20, 30, and 40 vol% were produced, and the 30 vol% scaffolds were selected for characterization. All architectures retained TPMS geometries and exhibited interconnected pore networks with open porosities exceeding 55%, while the gyroid showed the highest shape fidelity. Degradation rates decreased from 0.070–0.087 mm/year at day 7 to 0.039–0.052 mm/year at day 28, with the diamond degrading slowest. Before immersion, the diamond exhibited the highest compressive strength (5.5 ± 0.4 MPa) and elastic modulus (0.67 ± 0.19 GPa). During immersion, compressive strength increased due to corrosion-product deposition. Finite element and computational fluid dynamics analyses revealed architecture-dependent mechanical and transport behavior, with the gyroid showing the highest permeability and lowest pressure drop. All scaffolds supported preosteoblast attachment, with the gyroid showing the highest metabolic activity. These findings demonstrate that TPMS architecture strongly governs the structural, degradation, mechanical, transport, and biological performance of extrusion-printed Zn scaffolds.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning reveals a compact, low-dimensional geometric basis underlying sheet and skeletal TPMS architected materials
papers.abstract: Triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) architectures constitute one of the largest and most diverse families of architected materials, yet the geometric principles governing their mechanical and thermal behavior remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate fourteen TPMS topologies spanning both sheet- and skeletal-based realizations and characterize their geometry through a set of sixteen physically interpretable descriptors. Combining finite element simulations with explainable machine learning, we establish descriptor hierarchies for the effective mechanical and thermal properties across the TPMS design space. Surface area and compactness emerge as universal descriptors shared by both architecture classes, while descriptors of diminishing importance differ between sheet and skeletal networks, reflecting distinct manifestations of geometric heterogeneity. Despite these differences, a unified four-descriptor representation is identified that accurately predicts Young’s and shear moduli, thermal conductivity, as well as uniaxial and shear yield limits across all topologies for both network classes with coefficients of determination exceeding \(R^2=0.93\) . Interestingly, both principal component analysis (PCA) and the nonlinear Levina-Bickel intrinsic dimension estimator reveal that the geometric descriptor space and the associated performance space collapse onto a compact, nearly two-dimensional manifold, indicating that the apparent complexity of TPMS architectures arises from a remarkably low-dimensional organization. These findings provide a unified framework, applicable across sheet- and skeletal-based network classes, for interpretable modeling and materials informatics of TPMS architected materials, and establish a compact basis for future inverse-design methodologies.

papers.title: Human Osteoblast Behavior on Titanium Implant Surface Coating with Sintered Hydroxyapatite
papers.abstract: Osseointegration is strongly influenced by the physical and chemical characteristics of the implant surfaces, namely topography, roughness profile, and biofunctionalization. The current research assessed the influence of laser surface texturing and hydroxyapatite (HA) biofunctionalization on the viability, morphology, and inflammatory profile of human osteoblasts. Ti-6Al-4V disks were mechanically polished or laser-textured using an Nd:YVO4 laser to generate checkerboard patterns with spatial periodicities of 0.25 or 0.8 mm. Textured surfaces were subsequently coated with nanohydroxyapatite and sintered using either conventional furnace or CO2 laser sintering. The immortalized human osteoblastic line (hFOB 1.19) was seeded onto seven experimental surfaces for up to 14 days. Cell viability was assessed by a resazurin-based assay, while cellular attachment and morphological features were examined using scanning electron microscopy. Additionally, release levels of IL-1β, IL-8, and IL-10 were quantified by ELISA. Smooth titanium exhibited higher osteoblast viability than textured surfaces, whereas the 0.25 mm pattern generally performed better than the 0.8 mm pattern. HA biofunctionalization consistently improved viability within both texture patterns, irrespective of the sintering method, while the sintering technique itself had no significant effect. The 0.8 mm pattern showed lower IL-1β secretion, whereas IL-10 remained largely unchanged. Considering the inherent bounds of this in vitro study, smooth titanium surfaces exhibited the highest osteoblast viability, whereas the 0.25 mm pattern overall induced a more favorable cellular response compared to the 0.8 mm pattern. Hydroxyapatite biofunctionalization improved cell viability, whereas no consistent differences were observed between conventional and laser sintering.

papers.title: Tibiocalcaneal Arthrodesis for Ankle Arthropathy Using Patient-Matched Modular 3D-Printed Porous Titanium Implants and Locked Intramedullary Fixation
papers.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the clinical and radiographic outcomes of tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis using patient-matched modular 3D-printed porous titanium implants combined with locked intramedullary nails for advanced ankle arthropathy with substantial bone loss. Methods: This prospective cohort study included seven consecutive patients who underwent tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis using patient-matched modular 3D-printed porous titanium implants between January 2024 and December 2025. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM). Osseous union, alignment, and implant position were evaluated using radiographs and computed tomography at 1 year. Results: The mean patient age was 58.4 years (71.4% female). Mean follow-up was 12 months. Median reconstruction volume was 9,862 mm³ (interquartile range, 4,049–11,118 mm³). The median FAAM score improved from 60 preoperatively to 80 at 1 year (p = 0.018). At 1 year, complete osseous union was observed in two patients (28.6%), partial union in four (57.1%), and nonunion in one (14.3%). Complications occurred in three patients (42.9%): persistent nonunion with mechanical instability (n = 1), transient instability requiring supplemental fixation (n = 1), and superficial wound maceration that resolved with conservative care (n = 1). No major complications were reported. Conclusions: Patient-matched modular 3D-printed porous titanium implants combined with locked intramedullary nails may offer a limb-salvage option for advanced ankle arthropathy with massive bone loss. However, the high complication rate (42.9%) and low complete union rate (28.6%) at 1 year highlight the limitations of this approach. Long-term postoperative mechanical protection and regular monitoring are essential to prevent late structural failure.

papers.title: Spheroid-based generation of 3D myogenic tissues using transgene- and sorting-free differentiation of hiPSCs
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) represent a clinically relevant cell source for skeletal muscle tissue engineering, yet transgene-free maturation remains challenging. Moreover, the potential of spheroids as building blocks for muscle engineering remains poorly defined. This study evaluated whether hiPSC-derived myogenic spheroids enhance biofabrication outcomes in an in vitro bio-artificial muscle (BAM) system compared to a conventional single cell approach. Methods. CD56+ hiPSC-derived myoblasts were generated using a transgene-free protocol and differentiated toward 2D myotubes. In 3D, myoblasts were aggregated into 140-200 µm spheroids. Spheroids or single cells were encapsulated in a fibrin-based BAM, kept under tension using metal pins. Non-encapsulated spheroids and BAMs were cultured up to 15 days and evaluated for myosin heavy chain (MYH)+ organization, transcriptional profile, and contractile function. Results. In 2D, MYH+ myotubes showing multinucleation and, occasionally, sarcomere striation were formed. Spheroids were successfully generated, increased in size and circularity, and showed an enhancing MYH positivity, particularly during the proliferation phase, and displayed a fetal/perinatal myogenic state. In BAMs, spheroids promoted MYH positivity and established larger continuous MYH+ structures. Transcriptional profiles of spheroid and single cell BAMs were broadly similar. Tetanic forces were generally higher in spheroid BAMs; however, this difference did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion. hiPSC-derived myogenic spheroids advance MYH expression, but terminal maturation is constrained, likely due to their intrinsically isotropic nature. Within BAMs, spheroids enhance MYH+ myotube formation, but do not overcome limitations in myoblast fusion. Incomplete spheroid outgrowth and poor control over their spatial distribution are important challenges for their integration. Future work should focus on improving hiPSC differentiation efficiency, implementing spheroids in earlier differentiation stages, and optimizing spheroid outgrowth and positioning, alongside incorporating remaining muscle components as fibroblasts and vascular cells. This will refine whether spheroid-based assembly can add value in specific biofabrication contexts.

papers.title: Nutritional status, inflammatory burden, and CT-derived muscle phenotypes for predicting chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty: an explainable machine learning study
papers.abstract: Background Hip fracture (HF) is a common fragility fracture in older adults and may lead to persistent pain and impaired recovery. Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) after total hip arthroplasty (THA) negatively affects rehabilitation and quality of life. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model integrating clinical variables, peri-hip muscle characteristics, and nutrition-related inflammatory indicators for CPSP prediction after THA in patients with HF. Methods This single-center cohort study included patients with HF undergoing primary unilateral THA between October 2022 and March 2026. Patients from October 2022 to September 2024 were randomly divided into training and internal validation sets, while those from October 2024 to March 2026 served as an independent temporal test set. CPSP was defined as surgery-related pain persisting for ≥3 months with NRS ≥4. Candidate predictors included clinical, psychological, nutritional, inflammatory, and CT-derived muscle parameters. LASSO and Boruta were used for feature selection, and six machine learning algorithms were compared. SHAP analysis was applied to interpret the optimal model. Results Among 881 patients, 137/529 (25.9%) developed CPSP in the development cohort. Seven predictors were selected: GNRI, gluteus medius/minimus muscle density, gluteus medius/minimus cross-sectional area, NLR, age, preoperative anxiety, and PNI. The SVM model showed the best performance, achieving an AUC of 0.854 in the temporal test set, with accuracy of 0.770, sensitivity of 0.789, specificity of 0.763, NPV of 0.913, F1-score of 0.637, and Brier score of 0.125. SHAP analysis identified GNRI as the most influential predictor (35.4%), followed by muscle density (13.6%) and NLR (12.5%). Conclusions A machine learning model integrating clinical, CT-derived muscle, and nutrition-related inflammatory features showed good predictive performance for CPSP after THA in patients with HF and may support early risk stratification and individualized perioperative management.

papers.title: A variational physics-informed neural network framework for upper-bound plastic limit analysis of Mindlin plates
papers.abstract: This paper presents a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework based on the kinematic upper-bound formulation for rigid-perfectly plastic Mindlin plates. While PINNs have been increasingly adopted in computational mechanics, their capability to directly minimize the non-smooth plastic dissipation functional for evaluating structural collapse mechanisms has remained largely unexplored. By recasting limit analysis as a sampling-based neural variational optimization problem over admissible velocity fields, the proposed approach provides a mesh-free alternative to traditional finite element and second-order cone programming (SOCP) techniques. In this sampling-based variational framework, the transverse velocity and two independent rotation fields are approximated by neural networks, including both standard multilayer perceptrons and residual networks enriched with learnable Fourier feature embeddings. The von Mises plastic dissipation functional is integrated through the plate thickness by Gauss–Legendre quadrature and over the mid-plane by quasi-Monte Carlo integration, and is minimized subject to a unit external-work normalization. Essential kinematic boundary conditions are embedded through geometry-dependent hard constraints implemented by analytical masking functions and local projection operators. The unit-work condition is treated through work-normalization strategies, with penalty enforcement and explicit work normalization compared in the numerical study. Numerical studies are conducted for square, skew rhombic, circular, triangular, and hexagonal plates under clamped and simply supported boundary conditions. The results show that the proposed PINN formulation can reproduce the main collapse-load trends and dissipation patterns reported in reference upper-bound solutions, while the Fourier-enriched architecture generally improves the resolution of localized plastic dissipation. Furthermore, the thickness studies demonstrate that the continuous neural representation naturally mitigates the severe shear-locking phenomenon commonly associated with low-order Mindlin finite elements, maintaining robust collapse-load predictions even in the thin-plate limit. Finally, remaining sensitivities to network architecture, optimization effort, and geometric boundary treatments are identified and discussed.

papers.title: Additive versus Multiplicative Neuron Surrogates for Predicting the Structural Response of Steel Roof Trusses
papers.abstract: Neural network surrogates can replace repeated finite element runs in the design of steel roof trusses, but the choice of neuron model is rarely tested under controlled conditions. This study compares an additive Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with a Multiplicative Neuron Model (MNM) at matched capacity (211 and 196 free parameters). Both were trained on a parametric STAAD.Pro database of 46,140 Fink, Howe, Pratt and Warren trusses designed to IS 800:2007, with failing designs retained. Each network predicted eight continuous responses and the binary design status from nineteen inputs. On unseen test data the MLP reached a mean coefficient of determination of 0.942–0.946 across the four profiles, against 0.700–0.775 for the MNM. Its mean absolute percentage error was 11–17 %, against 26–37 %. Total weight was predicted best (R² ≥ 0.964 for the MLP) and the maximum utilisation ratio worst (R² ≈ 0.80–0.83), because the governing member changes across the design space. For design-status classification the MLP’s false negative rate was 0.074–0.213, against 0.210–0.608 for the MNM. Because the MNM used a bounded geometric-mean aggregation and slightly fewer parameters, its deficit is attributed to the multiplicative form itself, which fits the near-additive structure of truss responses poorly. The MLP is recommended as the surrogate, with the utilisation ratio treated as its least certain output.

papers.title: Technology-assisted rehabilitation after total hip arthroplasty: a systematic review of robot- and sensor-based interventions
papers.abstract: Introduction Robot- and sensor-based interventions are increasingly used in postoperative rehabilitation, but their clinical effects after total hip arthroplasty (THA) remain unclear. Methods Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance, we searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for randomised controlled trials evaluating robot- or technology-assisted physiotherapy delivered in the postoperative phase after THA. Three reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane tool. Results From 181 records, three trials met eligibility criteria. Interventions included an exoskeleton (Hybrid Assistive Limb), a visualized loading-control robot combined with conventional rehabilitation, and an electromyography-based (EMG-based) rehabilitation robot. Compared with conventional rehabilitation, robot- or technology-assisted interventions showed signals of short-term benefits in pain, hip range of motion (particularly hip extension), functional scores, and walking endurance in some studies, whereas walking speed and maximal strength outcomes were inconsistent. Quality of life improved in one trial despite no between-group difference in maximal strength. Conclusions Evidence for the efficacy of robot- or technology-assisted postoperative rehabilitation after THA is limited and heterogeneous. Current trials suggest potential early benefits for selected outcomes, but firm conclusions are precluded by a small number of studies, variability in devices and dosing, and short follow-up. Well-designed, adequately powered trials with standardised outcomes are needed.
